candidats.titre: Un monde, un regard — Guy Savoy, le grand roman de la cuisine
candidats.resume: Il est l'un des chefs les plus célèbres de la planète. Et pour cause : pour la neuvième année consécutive, son restaurant situé à La Monnaie de Paris a été sacré meilleur restaurant du monde. Chez lui, l'exigence commence dès la sélection des ingrédients, mais le plaisir va bien au-delà de l'assiette. Manger est une expérience totale. S'attabler dans son restaurant, c'est aussi s'immerger dans un univers où l'art culinaire côtoie des oeuvres d'art, dans un cadre unique. Aujourd'hui, alors qu'il publie un livre sur les auteurs du XIX siècle, il revient au micro de Rebecca Fitoussi pour évoquer ces ouvrages qui placent la nourriture au coeur du roman. Que retient-il de l'amour de la cuisine d'un Émile Zola ou d'un Chateaubriand ? Comment rend-il hommage au patrimoine littéraire dans ses recettes ? Et surtout, l'art de la table peut-il rivaliser avec les plus grands romans ? Et d'où lui vient cet optimisme malgré la morosité de l'époque ? candidats.titre: Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention -- by Philip Strahan, Tuo Yang
candidats.resume: The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for banks.

candidats.titre: Espagne : la « priorité nationale », une réponse à la crise du logement qui pourrait l’aggraver
candidats.resume: Une femme traite un dossier de demande de visa à son bureau. Pressmaster/Shutterstock L’ESSENTIEL Le parti espagnol d’extrême droite Vox place la « priorité nationale » au centre de son programme pour les législatives espagnoles de novembre. Dans la région de Valence, ce principe impose déjà plusieurs années d’inscription au registre des habitants pour accéder au logement aidé. Cette politique ne traite pas les causes de la pénurie et risque de diviser des locataires aux difficultés semblables. La pénurie de logements et l’envolée des loyers sont au cœur des prochaines élections générales en Espagne (les législatives du 29 novembre). Alors que chaque parti présente aux électeurs ses pistes pour sortir de la crise, le parti d’extrême droite Vox défend une solution simple : le principe de prioridad nacional , ou « priorité nationale », qui placerait les Espagnols en tête de file pour bénéficier des prestations publiques. Cette mesure occupe une place centrale dans le programme de Vox. Celui-ci prévoit de développer le logement social en donnant la priorité aux ressortissants espagnols, tout en misant sur la dérégulation et les baisses d’impôts. Présentée comme une solution de bon sens, la priorité nationale ne s’attaque pourtant pas aux causes profondes de la pénurie. Elle pourrait même les aggraver. La crise du logement , comme bien des crises, fait des gagnants et des perdants : pendant que les locataires sont à la peine, les propriétaires bailleurs encaissent des loyers plus élevés et voient la valeur de leur patrimoine grimper. La priorité nationale ne change rien à ces…

candidats.titre: En Australie, l’immigration recule, mais l’inquiétude grandit : pourquoi les chiffres ne suffisent pas
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL Fin juin 2026, 55 % des Australiens jugeaient trop nombreux les migrants arrivant chaque année, sept points de plus qu’en 2024. Or, le solde migratoire du pays est en baisse depuis 2023. Cette hausse accompagne l’essor du parti anti-immigration One Nation, qui a réussi avec la droite à imposer l’idée d’une « crise migratoire ». S’en tenir aux chiffres ne suffira donc pas. Ainsi, au Royaume-Uni, la moitié des habitants croit l’immigration en augmentation alors qu’elle a baissé. En Australie, le solde migratoire net (l’écart entre les entrées et les sorties de personnes qui s’installent dans le pays ou le quittent durablement) est en baisse. Il a atteint un pic en 2023 et, à la mi-2026, il avait reculé de 45 %. L’opinion a pourtant évolué en sens inverse. Selon le sondage 2026 du Lowy Institute (un groupe de réflexion indépendant de Sydney, consacré aux questions internationales), publié fin juin, 55 % des Australiens estiment que le nombre de migrants qui arrivent chaque année en Australie est trop élevé. C’est un record pour cette enquête, en hausse de deux points sur un an et de sept points par rapport à 2024. Ainsi, à mesure que l’immigration recule, l’inquiétude qu’elle suscite grandit. Les chiffres et le poids politique du sujet suivent des trajectoires opposées. Ce phénomène montre combien il est vain de s’en tenir aux seuls chiffres dans les débats sur l’immigration . candidats.titre: Débat sur les migrations : pourquoi montrer les données ne suffit pas forcément à convaincre
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL En Europe, les décideurs écoutent la recherche, mais l’opinion et les pressions politiques façonnent aussi les décisions migratoires. Des résultats exposés avec neutralité peuvent aider à instaurer la confiance des citoyens européens, dont les inquiétudes et les valeurs sont à prendre en compte. Les chercheurs peuvent avoir davantage d’influence en endossant le rôle d’intermédiaires impartiaux, exposant les options disponibles. Travailler sur les migrations peut se révéler franchement frustrant. Vous pouvez consacrer des années à interroger des gens, à collecter des données, à tester des théories et à aboutir à ce qui vous semble être des résultats solides, pour finalement avoir l’impression que personne ne vous écoute. Les sempiternels arguments et idées reçues refont surface dans les débats publics , sans grand rapport avec les connaissances que vous et d’autres chercheurs avez établies. L’enjeu est important à plus d’un titre, notamment parce que les migrations occupent une place majeure dans les élections en Europe, en Amérique du Nord et ailleurs. Pourquoi, alors, le public ne prête-t-il pas attention à ce que disent les spécialistes ? Les chercheurs déploient beaucoup d’efforts pour comprendre ces questions, mais cela ne semble modifier ni ce que pensent les gens ni ce que font les gouvernements. Les chercheurs disposent pourtant de données solides, mais si les responsables politiques ne les écoutent pas, il peut en résulter des politiques mal conçues, voire contre-productives. La solution consisterait peut-être à se retrousser les manches, à multiplier…

Former OpenAI researcher says he found Nvidia Blackwell fingerprints hidden inside six Chinese AI models
AI researcher Will DePue says a forensic analysis has turned up the first technical evidence that leading Chinese AI labs have access to Nvidia's latest Blackwell hardware despite US export controls. He says senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have already checked the method.
According to a forensic investigation by Will DePue, Chinese AI companies DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group are using Nvidia's export-controlled Blackwell GPUs. DePue played a key role at OpenAI in building the Sora and Sora 2 video models as well as GPT-4o, o3, and GPT-5 before founding the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs.
His analysis, he says, provides the first technical evidence of this access. US officials and news outlets had suspected that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips but never published proof. DePue wrote on X that senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have already independently checked and confirmed his findings. According to DePue, six Chinese models released since April 2026 carry the distinct signature of Nvidia's Blackwell generation, while earlier models such as DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2.5 show traces of Nvidia's older Hopper generation.
The evidence comes directly from the published language models. An AI model consists of billions of numerical values called weights. Before training starts, PyTorch, the standard software framework, fills these empty slots with random numbers generated from a starting value called a seed. To distribute this massive amount of data quickly, the GPU splits the work across its individual compute cores. Because different chip models have different core counts, the filling process produces a characteristic pattern, according to the report. Older Hopper chips such as the H100 and H800 use 132 compute cores, while the newer Blackwell chips use exactly 148 or 152 cores depending on the model (B200/B300 or GB200/GB300).
Training then adjusts these values millions of times, but some slots for unused words or symbols keep their initial random values. Even in heavily trained parts of the model, a faint statistical echo of the initial distribution survives, according to DePue. He says he worked the pattern backward and reproduced the results for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3 exactly on real Blackwell chips. He has published the verification code on GitHub.
Training runs costing more than half a billion dollars
The analysis maps DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 to B200 or B300 chips (148 cores). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro, and Ant Group's Ling-3.1-flash show, according to the analysis, the 152-core pattern of Nvidia's liquid-cooled GB200 or GB300 flagship rack systems. DePue says chance can be ruled out statistically and that the method correctly identified all 24 control models with known hardware, including Meta's Llama 3.1 (H100).
DePue's report estimates that the five training runs he examined required about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs combined, as much computing power as roughly 30,000 older H100 chips. Kimi K3 alone required an estimated 4,500 Blackwell processors over about 70 days, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro about 3,000. At a unit price of about $70,000, each of those clusters would cost $200 million to $300 million, and all five systems together more than half a billion dollars.
The findings also align with analysis from Dylan Patel, chief analyst at SemiAnalysis. In an interview with Sequoia Capital, Patel said DeepSeek-V3's model architecture was still specifically tailored for Nvidia's Hopper chips, while DeepSeek-V4's architecture was built for Blackwell GPUs and Huawei's Ascend chips. According to DePue's report, models from other Chinese labs, including Alibaba's Qwen3.8 and those from Zhipu, Tencent, Xiaomi, and StepFun, still show only Hopper signatures, while Meituan's LongCat-2.0 points to Huawei hardware.
The fingerprint doesn't prove a legal violation
Strictly speaking, the method shows only which hardware initialized the weights, though the training itself very likely ran on the same systems. The only other technical explanation would be an AMD MI300X, which is also restricted, artificially throttled so it produces the same pattern. DePue says he ruled out AMD for DeepSeek-V4-Flash using tiny rounding differences between the chips.
The data doesn't reveal where the GPUs are or who owns them, according to the investigation. Because Chinese companies can rent computing capacity at data centers outside China, the report says its technical evidence shows access to Nvidia's top hardware but does not by itself prove physical smuggling or a violation of US export law.

The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.
“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.
The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.
However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

Anthropic's Claude for Manufacturing plugs AI directly into factory software to automate industrial workflows
Anthropic has released Claude for Manufacturing, a plugin giving the AI direct access to industrial software to automate factory workflows. The new solution connects via four universal interfaces to Autodesk Fusion, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft 365, and Infor. Other systems can be integrated through file exports to Microsoft 365.
With 17 specific skills, the AI drafts quotes from actual inventory, compares suppliers, generates quality reports and design variants, and analyzes sensor data and manuals during machine downtime. Via an added Infor plugin, Claude can also order from backup suppliers when deliveries are delayed and reschedule production—after human approval. All results are linked to original source documents for employee review before reaching customers or suppliers.
The plugin is available to Team and Enterprise customers but doesn't control physical machines yet. For that, Anthropic is separately developing the Model Hardware Standard as a research preview, connecting AI agents to devices like robotic arms and microscopes via standardized drivers. This cuts setup time from weeks or months to hours or minutes but still requires human oversight due to the AI's limited grasp of physical processes.

Nearly 70 percent of US agencies use generative AI, and unions are finally catching up with guardrails
US public-sector unions are winning more protections against AI surveillance and automation-driven job losses. The issue is growing more urgent as nearly 70 percent of US government agencies already use generative AI, according to an Ernst and Young survey.
The wins are piling up nationwide. After a strike vote in October, IFPTE Local 21 in Oakland secured retraining programs instead of AI-related layoffs. In Pennsylvania, Governor Josh Shapiro guaranteed SEIU Local 668 human oversight during a pilot of OpenAI's ChatGPT Enterprise. The Transport Workers Union in Ohio won veto power over autonomous vehicles. On top of that, California Governor Gavin Newsom banned AI surveillance software, often called "bossware," along with automated firings in September. New York has protected state employees from AI displacement by law since late 2025.
Employers are pushing automation to cut costs, according to labor researcher Kung Feng at UC Berkeley. Union leaders like Liz Shuler of the AFL-CIO, Lorena Gonzalez, and TWU's John Samuelsen support AI safety systems where they help workers but insist on mandatory human control over every AI application in the workplace, the Guardian reports.

Il n’est pas toujours aisé de démêler ce qui, dans le passage à l’acte d’un terroriste, relève de sa radicalisation idéologique et de ses éventuelles fragilités psychologiques. Dans le cas de Kevin Tessier, l’auteur de l’attentat raciste commis le 23 octobre à Trappes et La Verrière (Yvelines), ces deux ingrédients semblent avoir bouillonné durant plusieurs années jusqu’à exploser dans un déchaînement de violence raciste inouï, un périple meurtrier de vingt minutes qui a fait un mort et sept blessés.
Les auditions, dont Le Monde a pris connaissance, des proches de ce technicien en station-service de 39 ans, entendus en garde à vue dès le lendemain de l’attentat, racontent toutes un même cheminement funeste : celui d’un enfant perturbé depuis son plus jeune âge, devenu un jeune homme accro au cannabis et en proie à des « délires » paranoïaques, dont la haine et la violence, alimentées par certains discours médiatiques et politiques, se seraient peu à peu cristallisées à la maturité sur la figure de l’étranger.

« Il faut que ça s’arrête ! » Près de 2 200 chefs d’établissement, de source syndicale, ont manifesté vendredi 13 novembre dans une trentaine de villes pour exprimer leur désarroi face aux violences croissantes qu’ils subissent dans le cadre du mouvement lycéen. De tels rassemblements de personnels de direction – des fonctionnaires loyaux et discrets – n’avaient pas eu lieu depuis vingt ans.
Après avoir tenu à bout de bras leurs établissements pendant des semaines, les proviseurs des lycées mobilisés sont « à bout ». Plus de 80 ont été blessés depuis la mi-septembre quand d’autres ont reçu des insultes ou des menaces de mort. « Plus les jours passent, plus il y a des blessés et plus on craint le pire. A quel moment va-t-il y avoir l’incident de trop ? », se demande Bruno Bobkiewicz, secrétaire général du SNPDEN-Unsa, le syndicat majoritaire des personnels de direction, lors d’une conférence de presse organisée en liaison avec plusieurs rassemblements.
Par le biais de ces rassemblements, les chefs d’établissement veulent « adresser un message solennel aux lycéens et à l’opinion publique pour dire “stop !”. Convergence de différents mots d'ordre, important dispositif policier… A quoi s'attendre pour la journée de mobilisation du samedi 14 novembre ?
La coordination des gilets jaunes et des organisations de jeunesse appellent à défiler samedi "contre la vie chère". D'autres manifestations – pour le climat, contre les violences policières ou les violences faites aux mineurs – sont aussi prévues. A Paris, un cortège unique défilera entre les places de la République et de la Nation.
La mobilisation va-t-elle reprendre de la vigueur ? La coordination des gilets jaunes et plusieurs organisations de jeunesse ont appelé à manifester dans toute la France "contre la vie chère", samedi 14 novembre, pour un cinquième week-end consécutif. La semaine précédente, les manifestations avaient rassemblé 146 000 personnes en France, selon le ministère de l'Intérieur, et 250 000 selon l'intersyndicale de la jeunesse, une mobilisation en recul par rapport aux précédentes journées. La multiplicité des mots d'ordre et l'absence d'encadrement syndical font craindre aux autorités des troubles à l'ordre public dans la capitale. Franceinfo fait le point.
Pas d'appel à la mobilisation de la part des centrales syndicales nationales
L'appel à manifester est cette fois porté par l'intersyndicale de la jeunesse et les gilets jaunes, et est relayé localement par des unions régionales ou départementales de syndicats de salariés. Les branches d'Ile-de-France de la CGT, de la FSU et de FO participeront ainsi au cortège parisien, assure à l'AFP Vincent Gautheron, secrétaire général de l'union régionale CGT. En revanche, les confédérations syndicales nationales du secteur public et du secteur privé concentrent leur appel à la grève et aux manifestations sur la journée du mardi 17 novembre.
"Pour nous, c'est toujours plus inquiétant parce que ça veut dire que les cortèges ne sont pas encadrés", a estimé vendredi sur LCI le ministre de l'Intérieur. Laurent Nuñez redoute que "la main [soit] laissée aux organisations syndicales étudiantes, lycéennes, (...) qui ont moins d'expérience, qui ne déclarent pas toujours d'ailleurs" leurs manifestations.
Des revendications multiples
La coordination des gilets jaunes, qui contribue depuis le 17 octobre à l'organisation de manifestations les samedis dans toute la France pour dénoncer la "vie chère", appelle à un "acte V". La carte collaborative du mouvement recense jeudi à la mi-journée près de 230 actions pour la journée de samedi.
Le collectif enfantiste a par ailleurs prévu de manifester le même jour "contre les violences faites aux enfants et aux ados". Différentes organisations opposées à la proposition de loi sur la présomption d'usage légitime des armes par les forces de l'ordre dénonceront dans la rue, elles, "un permis de tuer". Le mouvement qui a organisé le 26 septembre des marches pour le climat a aussi prévu de défiler samedi "pour le présent et l'avenir des enfants".
Les cortèges devraient donc converger dans certaines villes, notamment Paris, où ils s'élancent tous de la place de la République pour rejoindre la place de la Nation. "Dans beaucoup d'endroits, par pression des préfectures, toutes les mobilisations auront un parcours commun ou un seul point de rassemblement", a assuré Benjamin Ball, membre de la coordination des gilets jaunes, à l'AFP. De son côté, Laurent Nuñez assurait vendredi sur LCI prévoir "entre 50 ou 60 défilés sur l'ensemble du territoire national".
Des risques d'"affrontements avec les forces de l'ordre", selon le ministre de l'Intérieur
Au niveau national, il existe "le risque de voir plusieurs cortèges non autorisés susceptibles de rechercher l'affrontement avec les forces de l'ordre et de se rendre dans les centres-villes", écrit le ministre de l'Intérieur dans un télégramme aux préfets daté de lundi et consulté par France Télévisions. "Aussi, je vous demande de ne pas baisser la garde face à des phénomènes plus éclatés voire sporadiques dont le niveau de violence ne baisse pas en intensité", ajoute Laurent Nuñez.
Dans la capitale, les autorités font état de "risques de troubles à l'ordre public", selon une note de la direction du renseignement de la préfecture de police de Paris, consultée par France Télévisions. Entre 30 000 et 60 000 manifestants sont attendus dans la capitale samedi, selon ce document. Parmi eux, 200 à 400 gilets jaunes et 500 à 1 000 militants contre les violences faites aux enfants.
La marche contre les violences policières devrait donner "une très forte coloration anti-police" à cette nouvelle journée de mobilisation. "Sujet fédérateur de l'extrême gauche radicale, de l'ultragauche et de la jeunesse des quartiers, une participation importante de cette population est attendue avec des discours hostiles aux forces de l'ordre pouvant se traduire par la constitution d'un bloc radical de 300 à 600 personnes en pré-cortège", estime la note de la préfecture de police, qui rappelle "le contexte social marqué par la tenue du procès médiatisé" du passage à tabac de Michel Zecler par des policiers. Les renseignements anticipent ainsi des "provocations verbales et physiques contre le dispositif policier, voire des dégradations ou des pillages".
Quelque 70 000 policiers et gendarmes mobilisés
En vue de cette journée, 70 000 policiers et gendarmes seront mobilisés, a annoncé le ministre de l'Intérieur sur LCI. "On aura le même dispositif que samedi dernier" et depuis le 24 octobre, a fait savoir Laurent Nuñez, précisant néanmoins que ce chiffre serait affiné lors d'une réunion vendredi. "C'est un dispositif qui est mobile, réactif, qui s'adapte à ce que font les groupes à risque, qui s'éclatent en petits groupes et qui essaient de contourner le dispositif des forces de l'ordre", a-t-il développé.
Des "contrôles dans la profondeur qui s'avèrent extrêmement dissuasifs" seront mis en place, comme lors des samedis précédents, a aussi prévenu le ministre. "Et comme je le dis à chaque fois, pour tout ce qui est casseurs et pilleurs, on les attend de pied ferme."
Pour éviter les débordements, Laurent Nuñez a également demandé aux préfets de "prendre les mesures de police administrative nécessaires", tout en mettant en place des contrôles de flux en amont des rassemblements, un prépositionnement de forces mobiles et des "interventions systématiques en cas d'atteintes contre les personnes et les biens". Concernant l'usage des grenades policières, il n'y a "pas de restriction de principe sur les moyens employés mais un usage proportionné conformément au cadre légal et réglementaire en vigueur", a-t-il rappelé.

Ce jeudi 12 novembre, les sénateurs ont validé le nouveau mode de calcul des allégements de cotisations patronales sur l’emploi. Les entreprises devront ainsi verser 2,8 milliards d’euros supplémentaires aux organismes sociaux en 2027, soit 900 millions de moins que ce que prévoyait le gouvernement dans son projet de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale. Et pour cause : la version du Sénat – provisoire à ce stade – prévoit une entrée en vigueur du nouveau mécanisme au 1er avril.
Budget de la Sécu : le Sénat supprime la taxe de 2,05% sur les mutuelles
Rejeté à une écrasante majorité, par 339 voix pour, et seulement une contre. Ce vendredi 13 novembre, en milieu de matinée, les sénateurs ont supprimé l’article 12 du projet de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale (PLFSS), qui prévoit de reconduire sur l’année 2027 la taxe de 2,05 % instaurée en 2026 sur les mutuelles, au bénéfice de la branche maladie de la Sécu. Dans un rare moment d’unité gauche-droite, l’ensemble des élus, tous bords confondus, est monté au créneau contre le gouvernement, dénonçant à la fois la reconduction d’une mesure initialement présentée comme « exceptionnelle », et son impact sur les finances des adhérents.
« Alors que notre pays affiche déjà un taux record de prélèvements obligatoires, l’augmentation continue des tarifs des mutuelles pénaliserait particulièrement le pouvoir d’achat des Français », a épinglé le sénateur LR Serge Berard. « Les assurés ne sont pas dupes, in fine, ce sont eux qui vont payer cette taxe. De grâce, renoncez à cette taxe, ne soyez pas étonnés que les Français perdent confiance en leur gouvernement avec des mesures de cette nature, qui en plus durent dans le temps. »
Une mesure décriée
La communiste Cathy Apourceau-Poly a rappelé « qu’en 2026, le législateur avait prévu un gel des cotisations pour éviter que les organismes ne reportent cette taxe sur leurs adhérents, mais que ce gel a été censuré par le Conseil constitutionnel ». Patrick Kanner, le président du groupe socialiste, a dressé un parallèle entre « l’augmentation de 8,2 % » du montant des cotisations payées en 2024 aux mutuelles par leurs adhérents, contre une hausse « de 5,4 % pour les prestations versées ». « Il y a manifestement pour les mutuelles un gain potentiel », a-t-il raillé.
Pour sa part Edwige Diaz, la présidente du groupe Union nationale pour les territoires, qui rassemble les élus RN et UDR du Sénat, a dénoncé une mesure « qui revient à alourdir le coût du travail », dans la mesure où l’employeur prend en charge une partie du coût de la mutuelle de ses salariés.
Un rendement de 1 milliard d’euros
Face à ce chœur des récriminations, la ministre de la Santé, Stéphanie Rist, s’est trouvée bien seule pour défendre la prolongation du dispositif, supposé rapporter la bagatelle de1,12 milliard d’euros dans un contexte de forte dégradation des comptes publics. « Oui, c’est vrai, cette contribution devait être exceptionnelle. Mais il est vrai aussi que depuis 2026 la situation géopolitique et les déficits de notre pays ont évolué. Comme vous le savez nous voulons atteindre un déficit à 5 % ».
Pour éviter d’alourdir l’ardoise, le rapporteur général Olivier Henno a indiqué que la commission des Affaires sociales allait compenser la suppression de cette taxe en proposant un transfert de charges, c’est-à-dire une bascule de certaines dépenses du ressort de l’Assurance maladie obligatoire vers les complémentaires, en particulier en ce qui concerne la prévention. « Cette mesure n’apportera pas le rendement de 1 milliard initialement prévu », lui a répondu Stéphanie Rist.
L’examen du projet de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale se poursuit jusqu’en début de semaine prochaine au Sénat, avant un vote solennel prévu mercredi. Le texte fera ensuite son retour à l’Assemblée nationale, où les députés l’ont rejeté en première lecture.

Le Sénat loin d’être convaincu par plusieurs propositions du budget de la Sécu 2027. Les élus ont affiché leur désaccord avec plusieurs taxes, dont une contribution demandée aux mutuelles, devant rapporter plus d’un milliard d’euros à l’Assurance maladie.
Dominée par une alliance entre la droite et les centristes frileuse face aux mesures fiscales, la chambre haute a affiché ses désaccords avec le gouvernement sur le projet de loi de financement de la Sécurité sociale (PLFSS).
« Taxe indirecte » sur les consommateurs
Principale décision sénatoriale, le refus quasiment unanime d’une contribution exceptionnelle sur les complémentaires santé, fixée à 2,05 %. Mise en place l’année dernière, elle devait être éphémère mais le gouvernement veut la reconduire pour récupérer 1,1 milliard d’euros.
« L’augmentation continue des tarifs des mutuelles pénaliserait particulièrement le pouvoir d’achat des Français », a dénoncé le sénateur Serge Bérard (Nouvelle Energie), fustigeant comme la plupart de ses collègues une « taxe indirecte » probablement répercutée par les mutuelles sur leurs adhérents.
Soucieux de préserver le déficit de la Sécu, les sénateurs assurent qu’ils pourront compenser ce milliard perdu en proposant un transfert de charges de l’Assurance maladie vers les mutuelles, notamment sur les dépenses de prévention. Mais la ministre de la Santé, Stéphanie Rist, a affirmé qu’il serait impossible d’obtenir un tel « rendement », défendant la taxe comme une mesure de « sérieux budgétaire ».

Laurent Nuñez promet aux policiers une revalorisation de leur prime de risque, les syndicats insatisfaits
Cette proposition faite par le ministre de l'Intérieur lors d'une réunion vendredi place Beauvau est jugée "insuffisante", voire "inadmissible", par les syndicats.
Le ministre de l'Intérieur a proposé aux syndicats, vendredi 13 novembre, une revalorisation de l'indemnité de sujétion spéciale de la police (ISSP), leur prime de risque, après plus d'un mois de blocages de lycées et d'universités, ainsi que des manifestations, qui ont mobilisé d'importants dispositifs des forces de l'ordre.
"Compte tenu des risques inouïs auxquels sont exposés actuellement les policiers et les gendarmes", rapporte le ministère de l'Intérieur après cette rencontre, Laurent Nuñez "a tenu à présenter aux organisations représentatives un plan de revalorisation de l'indemnité de sujétion spéciale, qui n'avait pas été revalorisée depuis 2019".
Cette revalorisation, qui porterait le taux de cette prime à 33,5%, "se ferait sur trois ans, jusqu'en 2029, avec une première marche en avril 2027. Sur cette base, les discussions se poursuivent", assure dans un message à la presse le ministère, soulignant le "contexte budgétaire contraint".
"Ce n'est pas tolérable, c'est même inadmissible"
"Le calendrier ne va pas. C'est insuffisant", a réagi le secrétaire général d'Unsa Police, Thierry Clair. "Le ministre nous dit que le sujet est toujours sur la table, qu'il espère faire mieux. On lui souhaite vraiment de faire mieux. Parce que pour le coup, ça ne nous satisfait pas du tout", a abondé Grégory Joron, secrétaire général d'Un1té.
"Ce n'est pas tolérable, c'est même inadmissible. J'allais même dire que c'est indécent de se retrouver dans une telle situation. J'ai l'impression de mendier et, croyez-moi, j'ai presque honte. Je suis triste pour tous mes collègues ce soir, a également lancé le secrétaire général d'Alliance, Fabien Vanhemelryck. Je suis écoeuré." Appelant les autres organisations à "faire front pour défendre le métier de policier", Alliance a promis de durcir le ton la semaine prochaine, lançant sur X "un appel à toutes les grèves possibles et imaginables".
L'augmentation de la prime ISSP à un taux de 35% est réclamée par tous les syndicats de la police depuis plusieurs mois. Créée en 1958, elle est la résultante de la fusion des primes de risque et de danger. Elle est intégrée dans le calcul de la pension de retraite des fonctionnaires de la police nationale.

They came to discuss AI, but EU leaders spent most of their time during a summit in Dublin on Friday grappling with questions about Ukraine — namely who should represent them in future peace talks.
Despite plenty of disagreement about whether it should be a single person (and if so, who) or a collection of them, they managed to strike a deal: Future talks would involve national security officials from Germany, France, the U.K., Italy and Poland — the so-called E5 powers — plus representatives from the European Commission and European Council. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has lifted a nationwide ground stop that halted departing flights across the United States for more than four hours after a “communication issue” affected air traffic control centres.
The FAA announced at 8:15pm Eastern time on Friday (01:15 GMT on Saturday) that it had lifted the order, after it issued the ground stop hours earlier at 3:54pm (20:54 GMT).
Airlines face delays and cancellations as they get aircraft and crews back into position.
The FAA said in a post on X in the afternoon that there had been a “temporary telecommunications outage” and that, as a precaution, all flights were being halted.
International flights would be handled case by case, it added.
More than 10,000 flights were delayed and over 4,000 cancelled, according to FlightAware, CBS News reported.
Some 4,042 flights were in the air, heading to US airports, when the ground stop was ordered, according to the tracking site Flightradar24.
The communication issue affected all 22 air route traffic control centres, which guide aircraft.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication that the ground stop was triggered by a threat to the US.
“Everybody’s safe. The flights are accounted for,” he said. “This is not another 9/11.”
President Donald Trump had been briefed, he added.
Asked whether a planned rollout of a new AI tool meant to help air traffic controllers could be to blame, Mullin said officials have not ruled it out. “You just can’t rule out anything at this point. We are going through that process,” he said.
The FBI does not believe a cyberattack or criminal activity caused the failure, Bloomberg reported, citing an official familiar with the matter.
The cited official said investigators were examining whether a software update could have caused the outage, though the cause had not been determined.
Democratic Senator Tammy Duckworth has called for a “thorough and complete investigation” of the reported FAA communication issues.
“The safety of our skies is built on redundancies. Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation,” Duckworth wrote in a post on X.
“As Aviation Subcommittee Ranking Member, I’ll be demanding answers from the FAA,” she added.
The disruption is the latest sign of strain on the US air traffic control system, which has been beset by equipment failures, communications problems and shortages of controllers, as the FAA tries to replace ageing infrastructure.
Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the company behind the FAA’s AI-powered air traffic management system, said its technology was not responsible for the nationwide ground stop.
“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a post on X.
The FAA awarded ASI an $875m contract in June to develop and deploy the SMART system, which uses artificial intelligence to support air traffic management.
The agency announced an expansion of the system across its 22 air traffic control centres on November 10, just days before the nationwide flight suspension.
US rail service affected
Amtrak, the US national rail operator, announced that its website and app are showing error messages and that customers are having difficulty reaching a representative, as it faces higher-than-normal call volumes because of the nationwide disruption to air travel.
“We apologize for the error messages on both our website and app, as well as the difficulty reaching a representative,” Amtrak said in a post on X in response to a complaint.
“We’re currently experiencing higher-than-normal call volumes due to ongoing airline issues,” the company said.
It recommended that customers try the services later.
Pilot and former FAA safety team representative Kyle Bailey told Al Jazeera: “Whether you are an expert or not, the bottom line is we’re still trying to piece the puzzle together, and it would be impossible to have an answer to the issue quickly, in a few hours at least.”
“But it is very alarming what we saw, and possibly [rail operator] Amtrak is being affected too,” he added. “The FAA’s priority at the moment is keeping not only the American passenger safe, but everyone flying in the US flight system.”
Bailey said that “halting the flights on the ground is the safest thing to do until they could figure out what’s going on. If anybody says they think they know what’s causing this problem at such an early stage, they’re not being honest”.
Congress approved $12.5bn for the overhaul last year, and the Department of Transportation and the White House asked lawmakers on Friday for another $30.1bn.
This was the first nationwide US ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last time had been after the September 11, 2001, attacks.
US authorities have yet to determine the cause of the telecommunications outage that prompted the ground stop.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands plan to announce in Vienna an agreement with Rwanda to establish a center for the deportation of migrants who have no legal right to remain in the European Union. This was reported by Politico Europe, citing three sources familiar with the scheme.
Pilot center in Rwanda
The agreement is expected to be announced on Monday. It will apply only to asylum seekers who have exhausted all options for obtaining legal permission to reside in the EU and have been refused.
The five countries have regularly held meetings to prepare a mechanism for establishing centers outside the European Union's territory. They will be able to deport there people who have been ordered to leave the EU. The countries had previously stated that they intended to conclude the first agreements on such centers in 2026 and launch them the following year.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Conditions and concerns
The center in Rwanda is intended to become a pilot project. According to the publication, agreements with other countries and involving other EU members may emerge later.
A recent reform of EU rules allowed member states to conclude agreements on such centers provided that international human rights standards are observed. At the same time, the details of the scheme, including the nationality of the people who will be transferred, the conditions of their stay and oversight mechanisms, will depend on the specific agreement.
Human rights organizations warn that such centers could create risks of human rights violations outside the EU's oversight and legal mechanisms. In 2023, the UK Supreme Court ruled unlawful the British plan to send asylum seekers to Rwanda for the remote processing of their claims. The planned initiative by EU countries concerns people who have already been ordered to leave the bloc's territory.

What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — President Trump is confronting new realities nine months into the war with Iran that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict.
On Thursday, he waved away the need for a deal with Iran, saying the U.S. has billions of Iran's dollars frozen in overseas accounts.
"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money," he wrote in a Truth Social post.
Negotiations with Iran are stuck with mediator Qatar working to bridge the divide. Trump met Qatar's prime minister at the White House this week, and said afterward that Gulf Arab allies prefer "the status quo" of continued economic pressure on Iran. He wrote that while the U.S. remains "locked and loaded," an attack at this point "seems to be quite unlikely."
That's a pivot from his threats to carry out quick, intense strikes on Iran in the days before he had to contend with two election setbacks.
Trump's wartime ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he'd thrown his support behind, is on the cusp of being ousted from power after elections there.
Meanwhile, at home, Trump's party lost its majority in Congress in midterm elections. Vice President Vance blamed Republican losses on the unpopular war with Iran and the nature of U.S. relations with Israel.
With less room to room maneuver and Iran still defiant, Trump's strategy appears to be to keep things as they are, for now. That means the possibility of escalation still looms.
Senior UAE diplomat, Anwar Gargash, told an audience in the country's capital of Abu Dhabi this week that the region must "prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty, in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted."
Here's what keeping the status quo looks like.
Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz persists
Official Iranian social media accounts frequently post videos of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz for violating Iran's new rules requiring permission to navigate the waterway, which was open and free to ships before the war.
The U.S., meanwhile, is assisting oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz using a route that's close to Oman's coastline. While this has helped Arab states export their oil, it does not solve the bigger problem of how to bring back the pre-war production levels of other vital products like liquified natural gas, fertilizer and aluminum. Nor does a status quo allow countries like Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain to import goods to their ports.
The International Monetary Fund says Gulf Arab states are in economic recession as a result of the war, despite higher oil prices. It says Kuwait, Qatar and Iraq's economies are contracting approximately 16% this year. Bahrain's is down 11%.
More limited strikes that could rapidly escalate
The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region, leaving open the possibility of another planned military escalation.
This week, Iran unveiled what it says is a new underground missile production site.
The U.S. and Iran are also still occasionally carrying out tit-for-tat for strikes.
On Friday, Iranian media said the U.S. struck one of its islands in the Strait of Hormuz. It's an area where Iran has radars and drone launch sites. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit back, targeting an early warning U.S. radar in Bahrain.
Iran remains economically battered, starved of oil revenue
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week there's no need for military action against Iran at this stage because economic sanctions are doing the job.
"The pain that they're feeling is, eventually you have to eat. Eventually you have to be able to pay your own fighters and your own security forces," Rubio said.
There's also a U.S. naval blockade at sea barring Iranian ships from transporting oil to countries like China. This blockade, according to the U.S. military, has cut Iran off from at least $25 billion in revenue so far.
One of the biggest economic blows, though, has come from the United Arab Emirates. The UAE announced over the summer it was severing all economic and trade ties with Iran. The UAE had been among Iran's biggest trade partners and local bank accounts were allegedly used by Iran's supreme leader and Revolutionary Guard to move money around.
Meanwhile, the U.S. military's Central Command announced a new operation, dubbed "Iron Gate," with other U.S. government agencies, aimed at preventing Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons across its borders and the Caspian Sea.
War in Yemen intensifies, draws in more countries
Another consequence of the conflict with Iran is the resumption of all-out war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
The Houthis, who are not a direct proxy of Iran but are supported by it, say Saudi airstrikes across Yemen have killed scores of people in past months, including nearly 60 this past weekend, many of them women and children in a village near the capital Sana'a.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces daily missile and drone attacks by Houthis, including some this week that hit its key East-West pipeline carrying crude oil to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Another Houthi attack hit Saudi oil company Aramco's skyscraper headquarters in Riyadh's financial district.
Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have led to flights and high-profile events being canceled.
As the Yemen war drags on, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt are among the countries entering the fray with defensive support to Saudi Arabia. The U.S. is assisting with intelligence on the Houthis.
The United Nations says some 330,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the renewed fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis.
Efforts by mediators continue, neither side budges
Iran says it's prepared for a short-term pause on attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, but insists that seven demands be met before entering into direct talks over its nuclear program.
"The message has been only one thing. These seven items are on the table. Take it or leave it," Hamidreza Gholamzade, Tehran municipality spokesperson, told NPR.
These demands include lifting sanctions, ending the naval blockade, unfreezing Iran's dollars in overseas accounts and enforcing a ceasefire across all fronts, which includes halting Israeli attacks in Lebanon and Gaza.
Rubio has described the conditions as "absurd."
There's also discussion on diluting and moving Iran's enriched uranium abroad. However, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, told Iran's state broadcaster Wednesday: "We will not remove even a shred of enriched nuclear material from Iran."
It's another indication of the gridlock.
NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi in Antalya, Turkey, and Ahmed Abu Hamada in Cairo contributed reporting.

Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention
Philip Strahan and Tuo Yang
NBER Working Paper No. 35985
November 2026
JEL No. E4, G21
ABSTRACT
The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower 
bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-
sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited 
the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large 
depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy 
normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. 
We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for 
banks.
Philip Strahan
Boston College
Carroll School of Management
and NBER
philip.strahan@bc.edu
Tuo Yang
Boston College
tuo.yang@bc.edu
1 Introduction
Central banks initiated two unconventional monetary policies following the wreck-
age of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC). First, they committed to holding the short-term
policy rate at its zero lower bound for an extended period (ZLB); second, they initiated
Quantitative Easing (QE) to lower long-term rates directly. This paper shows that both
dimensions of unconventional policies shifted the composition of bank deposits toward
more rate-sensitive customers, making it costlier and riskier for banks to retain deposits
once policy normalized.
The ZLB policy led to interest-rate spread compression, both across banks (because
deposit rates collapsed toward zero) and between banks and money markets (because
money market rates also collapsed toward zero). As a consequence, rate-sensitive
liquidity demanders lost the incentive to move funds into high-rate substitutes for
traditional bank deposits, or between banks based on differences in offered interest
rates. This change both increased the flow of overall deposits into banks (see Figures
1 and 2) and also meant that allocation of deposits across banks lost its connection to
deposit rates. As shown in Figure 3, the composition of bank deposits shifted away from
interest-bearing time deposits and toward checkable, non-interest bearing accounts.
This compositional change in deposits, as a consequence of the ZLB, reflects inflows
from interest-sensitive customers, which emerge later when the short rate lifts off zero.
We show that this change in composition affected how deposit supply responded when
monetary conditions normalized.1
QE, or large-scale purchases by the Federal Reserve (“the Fed”) of long-term bonds,
also affected bank financing by mechanically increasing deposits when the bonds sold
originate from outside the banking system (Hancock and Passmore, 2015; Christensen
and Krogstrup, 2019, 2022; Acharya et al., 2024).2 This component of unconventional
1Unlike the Fed, the European Central Bank set its policy rate below zero. This policy created
additional funding problems for banks because they were unable to pass negative rates through fully to
depositors. See Heider, Saidi and Schepens (2019) for a discussion of the policy tradeoffs.
2Deposits created by QE enter into banks, with the reserves created diluting the average risk and
return of their asset portfolios. Banks thus rebalance themselves toward long-term bonds and other risky
assets such as loans, and the portfolio rebalancing activity reaches the wide universe of U.S. banks.
1
monetary policy increased the share of uninsured deposits at banks, as we show, thus
potentially harming funding stability. Uninsured depositors are both more interest-
rate sensitive on average than insured ones, and they also respond to solvency shocks
(because uninsured depositors are exposed to bank failure risk). This latter, latent risk
became manifest during the SVB run and collapse (Jiang et al., 2024; Drechsler et al.,
2026).
We estimate the effects on bank deposits of these two dimensions of unconventional
policy simultaneously, an exercise challenged by the fact that QE, by design, overlaps
with the ZLB. The two policies have different effects on bank stability — one potentially
changes interest-rate sensitivity (the ZLB), while the other affects that and also run
risk by increasing uninsured deposits (QE). But testing their effects separately poses a
challenge because central banks resort to QE only when they have reached the limit of
the standard monetary tool, the short-term money market rate, by putting that rate at
its zero lower bound. Hence, the two policies are inherently coincidental.
We are able to separate the effects of the two policies by exploiting a new instrument
which provides bank-market level variation in exposure to QE, following Yang (2026).
The instrument uses granular data on Fed bond purchases, which are publicly disclosed
at the transaction level. When these bond purchases originate from non-banks, they
mechanically increase deposits at banks, but they are always intermediated at the
original point of sale through a small number of large banks, the so-called Primary
Dealers (PDs). Hence, the initial deposits created are not randomly distributed across
the system. The instrument exploits the fact that non-PD banks with high market
overlap with the PDs experience deposit inflows due to these Fed bond purchases.3
And, the effect on deposits is strongest both statistically and economically for uninsured
deposits. Thus, we can construct a time-varying measure of sensitivity to QE at both
the bank and the bank-county levels.
Our core model relates deposit flows to deposit interest rates, to exposure to QE and
3This measure of QE exposure illustrates the Cantillon Effect, which argues that money creation has
non-neutral effects because it does not reach all economic agents at the same time, as the metaphorical
“helicopter drop” would.
2
its interaction with the deposit rate, and to exposure to ZLB and its interaction with the
deposit rate. Following Begenau and Stafford (2022), we measure the deposit rate using
their construct Rate Gap, which equals the difference between what a given bank pays
for deposits compared to the average amount paid by competing banks raising deposits
in the same local market(s). Rate Gap offers an exogenous (from the local market
perspective) measure of a given bank’s relative aggressiveness in pricing its deposits
because multi-market banks engage almost completely in uniform pricing across local
markets.4 As such, a bank’s relative deposit rate in a given market (compared to
competing banks in that same market) isolates the supply side and does not reflect
local funding demands (which in part drive local deposit growth apart from deposit
rates). We first replicate Begenau and Stafford (2022), who show that Rate Gap strongly
predicts deposit growth at the bank-county-year level (based on deposit growth in the
Summary of Deposits); we then extend their results to show that averaging Rate Gap
up to bank level (across local markets) provides a strong predictor of deposit growth at
the bank-quarter level.
Our model shows that during the ZLB, Rate Gap’s explanatory power for deposits
falls sharply, especially at banks heavily exposed to QE. This happens because spreads
compress toward zero (which is evident in the distribution of deposit rates as well
as in Rate Gap — see Figures 4 and 5), which shifts the composition of deposits from
interest-bearing accounts (especially time deposits) to non-interest bearing ones. Deposit
growth thus loses its connection to interest rates during the ZLB, as differences in rates
are just too small to matter. As such, deposits do not move across banks, and many
new deposits flow into banks generally from money markets because banks provide
marginally higher levels of protection and marginally higher levels of liquidity. Figure
1 shows that bank deposits grow rapidly relative to money market funds during the
ZLB, and the reverse happens outside the ZLB. Said differently, without a pricing edge,
money markets are at a severe competitive disadvantage relative to banks.
4For example, in 2019 the average US bank had over 100 branches but set just 1.1 unique interest rates
across those branches; see Table 1 from Begenau and Stafford (2022).
3
We then test how deposit dynamics change during the two most recent rate cycles,
one after the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and the other after the Pandemic. Once
interest rates lifted off the ZLB — first in late 2015 and again in 2022 — exposure
to QE increased interest-rate sensitivity of deposit flows. That is, banks with high
QE and ZLB exposure could only retain their deposits by increasing interest rates to
match changes in market conditions. We further show that exposure to both QE and
the ZLB increases bank deposit betas, which measure how aggressively banks raise
deposit rates in response to increasing market rates. Unconventional policy shifted the
composition of bank deposits toward interest-sensitive customers. As a result, when
interest rates increased off the zero lower bound, banks with high exposure to those
policies raised deposit rates more in order to help them retain those deposits, which
otherwise would seek higher yield (either in the money markets or at other banks).
Retaining deposits thus becomes more costly (i.e., higher deposit rates) and riskier (i.e.,
more rate sensitivity) due to banks’ exposure to unconventional policy.
Our paper contributes to several strands of the emerging literature on bank funding
during the post-GFC period.
First, the results speaks to the literature on the deposit franchise value. The seminal
work by Drechsler, Savov and Schnabl (2017) on the deposits channel of monetary policy
emphasizes the sensitivity of bank deposit supply to the spread between money market
rates and bank deposit rates. Banks earn rents on sticky deposits — which generates
the deposit franchise value — because this stickiness allows them to pay below-market
rates. We show that rate sensitivity collapsed from unconventional monetary policy,
leading to large deposit inflows. Despite these inflows, rate compression toward zero
meant that the deposit franchise value was reduced by unconventional monetary policy
(at least on a per-dollar basis). Yet when monetary conditions normalized, exposure
to deposits from unconventional policy eroded the natural interest-rate risk hedge to
offset asset-side losses with value generated by pricing deposits below market rates.5
5Drechsler, Savov and Schnabl (2021) report evidence from this natural hedge, but they do not
consider the two most recent interest rate upcycles where this hedge becomes less effective. Their analysis
ends in 2017.
4
In other words, banks heavily exposed to QE and to the ZLB had to raise deposit rates
in order to keep deposits from flowing out. Consistent with our arguments, Usenko
(2026) shows that interest rate sensitivity is highest among large depositors, exactly
those which we show are drawn into the banking system by unconventional monetary
policies.
Second, we extend Acharya et al. (2024), who argue that QE harmed bank stability
by increasing their exposure to liquidity risk, both in lending and in taking deposits.
They emphasize the asymmetry in liquidity exposure, whereby banks increase liquidity
risk during QE episodes (which is offset by the associated increase in reserves), but do
not lower this exposure when QE ends; this asymmetry results in more fragile banks as
a legacy of the QE programs. Our mechanism focuses on how unconventional policy
— both QE and the ZLB — affected deposit interest sensitivity during rate increasing
periods, which we show increases at banks most exposed to the two components of
unconventional policy.
Third, we contribute to the literature on fragility stemming from the Silicon Valley
Bank (SVB) crisis.6 This literature focuses mainly on SVB’s pathological combination of
long-term assets financed with almost 100 percent uninsured deposits. Jiang et al. (2024)
estimate large duration-related losses at SVB (like many banks) and show that they
had especially high levels of uninsured deposits, which increased fragility. Drechsler
et al. (2026) argue that the deposit franchise itself is fragile because it can support two
equilibria, one in which deposits stay in the bank and the bank earns rents on them
when market interest rates rise (because spreads rise), thus offsetting asset-side losses;
another equilibrium exists, however, in which depositors run under the rational belief
that the bank will become insolvent if other depositors leave. This mechanism neatly
explains the funding problem related to uninsured deposit fragility, but it does not
address the broader effect of deposit composition on interest rate sensitivity, which is the
focus of our paper. Blickle et al. (2025) is closest to our paper, as it shows higher deposit
6Cookson et al. (2026) emphasize the role of social media in amplifying and extending the effects of
the SVB run.
5
flightiness after unconventional policy. However, our paper, unlike theirs, exploits
cross-bank heterogeneity in exposure to both dimensions of unconventional policy. As
such, we can separate the effects of the two components of that policy: the extended
ZLB and large-scale asset purchases from QE.
2 Unconventional Monetary Policy
Monetary stimulus coming out of the Global Financial Crisis, based on reductions
in the short-term interest rate, was viewed as insufficiently powerful to stimulate the
economy and foreclose the possibility of a deflationary spiral like what had occurred
during the 1930s (Friedman and Schwartz, 1963; Bernanke, 1983). In part the problem
emerged from prior declines in interest rates, which had trended down since the middle
of the 1980s and thus reduced the policy space for the Fed to lower interest rates
(Hillenbrand, 2025). As a result, the Federal Reserve dropped its policy rate to near
zero in late 2008, and added two new tools to amplify its influence on overall financial
conditions. First, Forward Guidance was implemented by communicating the Fed’s
intent to leave the short rate at its “Zero Lower Bound” (ZLB) for an extended period
of time. Second, the Fed initiated large-scale asset purchases, aka Quantitative Easing
(QE), designed to put additional downward pressure on long-term interest rates by
buying long-term Treasuries and Mortgage-Backed Securities. The Fed reinstituted both
of these policies in response to the Pandemic.
Bernanke (2017) and Kuttner (2018) survey the policy rationales as well as the em-
pirical evidence about the effectiveness of these unconventional tools. A number of
studies find loosening of financial conditions such as declines in term premia around
policy announcements (e.g., Gagnon et al., 2011; Krishnamurthy et al., 2011; Ehlers, 2012;
Bauer and Neely, 2014) and increases in bank lending for more-exposed banks (Rod-
nyansky and Darmouni, 2017; Luck and Zimmermann, 2020; Chakraborty, Goldstein
and MacKinlay, 2020).7 Neither survey paper, however, considers how these policies
could affect banking stability when monetary conditions normalized.
7Diamond, Jiang and Ma (2024), in contrast, argue that QE constrained lending by filling up bank
balance sheets with reserves and thus displacing balance sheet capacity for lending.
6
We argue that both the persistent use of the ZLB as well as QE could increase
bank exposure to interest-sensitive deposits. Prior to this period, bank deposits had
been largely supplied by sticky customers with low interest elasticity.8 As a result,
deposit spreads increased when interest rates rose; although some deposits did flow
out, the wider spread provided banks with a hedge against losses from holding interest-
sensitive (i.e., long-term) assets like mortgages or mortgage-backed securities. The
utility of this natural hedge could decline with both the persistent ZLB and by QE
because both policies may change the interest sensitivity of bank deposits. Importantly,
this sensitivity only becomes evident when unconventional policy ends and monetary
conditions normalize.
The ZLB changes the composition of bank deposits because it leads to spread com-
pression. As illustrated in Figures 4 and 5, the variation across banks in deposit rates
declines sharply during these periods. Moreover, the difference in rates paid by the
median bank versus that paid by money markets also declines (Figure 6). Hence,
interest-sensitive liquidity demanders, for example corporate CFOs, lose the incentive
to search for yield on their short-term assets. Prior to the ZLB period, many such agents
would park cash in money markets rather than banks to receive higher returns (recall
Figure 1).9 With spread compression, bank deposits become a better option given the
stronger explicit and implicit insurance against losses. This helps explain the rapid
growth of deposits during the years following the GFC, when deposits grew about
twice as fast as nominal GDP (recall Figure 2).
QE as envisioned by Bernanke was tantamount to a swap between private banks
and the Fed of long-term assets for short-term bank reserves. In its basic form, the Fed
would simply purchase a bond from a bank, and pay for that by issuing new reserves
into the selling bank’s Fed account. As such, the selling bank’s liabilities are unaffected,
while its portfolio of assets becomes shorter in duration and higher in liquidity. The
8Argyle et al. (2025) show that high-balance deposits exhibit higher stickiness; Egan et al. (2025) also
show that depositor stickiness varies with deposit size and depositor demographics (age). Lu and Wu
(2026) show that depositor inattention increases stickiness and enhances bank market power.
9The model crashed badly during the week following Lehman Brothers, leading to a government
bailout of the money market industry.
7
policy effect works by moving duration risk from the private banking system to the
government.
The problem with the textbook model of QE, where the Fed’s actions only affect
banks, is that most of the long-term bonds purchased originated outside the banking
system. Carpenter et al. (2015) show, for example, that most of the bonds came from
households (which is a catch-all category from the US Flow of Funds which includes
hedge funds), insurance companies, pension funds, and brokerage firms. None of these
entities can accept reserves from the Fed as payments for bonds sold. Instead, they are
paid in deposits by one of the Primary Dealer banks, which interact directly with the
Fed and act as an intermediary between the original seller and the Fed. The PD banks
then resell the bond to the Fed in return for reserves. The deposits (and reserves) thus
start at one of the PDs but then move to other banks. The new money created by QE
propagates across the banking system gradually, with its largest immediate effects at
banks located near the PD bank locations. Hence, QE in practice is not a simple asset
swap between banks and the Fed; instead, it leads to an expansion of both the asset side
(i.e., more reserves) and the liability side (more deposits) of banks. These new deposits,
as we will show, are not distributed evenly across banks and do not behave similarly to
normal deposits created by private market forces.
3 Data
This section details the data sources used in this paper. Our analysis draws on four
sources. Bank-level financial information comes from the Federal Financial Institutions
Examination Council (FFIEC) Call Reports; branch-level deposit information comes
from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) Summary of Deposits (SOD)
Data; transaction-level data on the Federal Reserve’s open market operations, used to
construct our QE deposit-channel instrument, come from the Federal Reserve Bank
of New York’s Open Market Operations transaction data; and aggregate macroeco-
nomic time series come from Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED). The sample
spans 2001 through 2025, covering both the post-financial-crisis and the post-pandemic
8
zero-lower-bound episodes and the tightening cycles that followed each. Detailed
variable definitions and summary statistics are provided in Appendix Tables A.1 and
A.2, respectively.
3.1 FFIEC Call Report Data
Our bank-level analysis uses FFIEC Call Report data accessed through Wharton
Research Data Services (WRDS). This dataset provides comprehensive accounting
information from the Consolidated Reports of Condition and Income, which all insured
commercial banks are required to file each quarter. For each bank-quarter, we retain only
the most recent submission to incorporate amended filings. Because flow variables in
the Call Reports — such as interest expense on deposits — are reported on a year-to-date
basis, we transform them into discrete quarterly flows by subtracting the value from
the preceding quarter within the same fiscal year. From these records, we construct
each bank’s deposits, insured and uninsured deposits, total assets, and its deposit
rate, measured as annualized interest expense on deposits scaled by average deposits.
This yields a consistent quarterly panel of bank balance-sheet and deposit-pricing
outcomes.10
3.2 FDIC Summary of Deposits (SOD) Data
For our local, bank-county analysis we use the FDIC Summary of Deposits (SOD)
data, which provide branch-level deposits and geographic identifiers for all FDIC-
insured institutions. These data are released annually with a reporting date of June
30. We use them to construct, for each bank, the geographic distribution of its deposits
across counties and its deposit market share within each county. Aggregating branch
deposits to the bank-county-year level gives the local deposit measures used throughout
the paper and the predetermined deposit-market weights that underlie our bank-county
analysis.
10When a bank is involved in a merger or failure, we drop the bank-time or bank-county-time
observation which contains the structural change, as this often has a massive effect on rates of change.
9
3.3 FRED Data
We supplement our analysis with aggregate macroeconomic time series from FRED
to characterize the broader economic environment across monetary policy phases. These
series include total deposits at commercial banks, money market mutual fund assets,
nominal GDP, the Federal Funds rate, and the 3-month Treasury bill rate. We use these
data, along with the Federal Funds rate path, to construct our descriptive figures and
date zero-lower-bound episodes.
3.4 Federal Reserve Bond Purchase Data
To construct our core measure of QE’s effect on bank deposits, we use transaction-
level security trade data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s Open Market
Trading Desk. These data record every asset purchase and sale conducted with primary
dealers — the financial institutions authorized to transact directly with the Fed — and
include the trade and settlement dates, transaction type, par and dollar amounts, CUSIP,
and counterparty. Because the Fed’s large-scale asset purchases flowed thro

[…]

ocal markets to finance investment, see Gilje, Loutskina
and Strahan (2016) and Drechsler, Savov and Schnabl (2017).
25In Table A.4 we replace Rate Gap with its analog using only savings accounts; these results are
similar in sign-pattern to those reported in Table 5, but with somewhat smaller coefficients.
21
Column (4) of Table 5 introduces the SVB interactions, which in this case are based on
indicators set to one during 2023. Consistent with Table 3, the core results change little.
Also consistent with Table 4, the SVB shock sharply increases interest rate sensitivity.
Table 6 estimates the same bank-county specification separately for small and large

bank-quarter level, splitting by size allows the sensitivity of local deposit flows to the

the size distribution, since large and small banks differ in their local market power,

4.3 Deposit Rate Sensitivity when Monetary Conditions Normalize
Tables 3 through 6 show that deposit-flow sensitivity to the Rate Gap falls during
the ZLB era when QE Exposure is high. In the best-identified models which fully
account for bank-time deposit demand (Tables 5 and 6), the decline in rate sensitivity
happens widely across banks. These patterns suggest that the incremental deposits
flowing into banks are being distorted by unconventional policy. The ZLB, by creating
compression in rates both across banks and between banks and money markets (recall
Figures 4 and 6), may draw in funds from normally rate-sensitive customers who are
putting their liquidity into banks (rather than money markets) for the increased safety
and liquidity. The same argument goes through for deposits pulled into banks by QE.
Once rates move off zero, these deposits start to discriminate more than other deposits

To test these ideas, we need to capture cross-bank variation in exposure to both QE

our prior models captured the ZLB with a simple time-series indicator variable. Since
some banks raised more deposits than others during the ZLB quarters, we now exploit

and ZLB quarters are progressively replaced by non-ZLB quarters, the measure tends
toward zero; because it averages signed deposit changes, however, it need not decline
monotonically. QE Exposure is constructed analogously: it is the 12-quarter moving
average of bank b’s QE-driven deposit inflow, scaled by lagged assets. To ease the
comparisons, we standardize both measures to have zero mean and unit variance.

Banks choose the amount of deposits raised in response to lending and other investment

predetermined, plausibly exogenous variation in its exposure to the ZLB episode. Our

5 Conclusion
Both dimensions of unconventional monetary policy, we find, came with the unex-

normalized. When the Fed decided to lower the short-term policy rate to zero and
committed to leave it there, it did so following a financial crisis sufficiently reminiscent

monetary stimulus through its large-scale purchase of long-term bonds also seemed

deposits from new sources; deposits, for example, grew by 42% between 2010 and 2015

responses, policy makers should take into account their effects on bank funding stability.

Der Winter 2024 war eine Bewährungsprobe für die koreanische Demokratie. Am 3. Dezember verhängte Präsident Yoon Suk Yeol das Kriegsrecht und befahl Militär und Polizei, die Nationalversammlung zu besetzen. Er wollte verhindern, dass das Parlament seine Erklärung aufhebt – ohne Erfolg.
Zwei Tage später begannen die koreanische Verfassungsrechtslehr:innen, sich zu organisieren. Am 25. Dezember gründeten 110 Verfassungsrechtler:innen aus dem ganzen Land offiziell das „Constitutional Scholars Council for Enhancement of Korean Constitutionalism“, also einen Rat der Verfassungswissenschaft „zur Stärkung des koreanischen Konstitutionalismus“. In den folgenden Monaten schlug der Rat öffentlich verfassungsrechtliche Lösungen vor. Er veranstaltete Foren und öffentliche Seminare, online wie offline. Er veröffentlichte gemeinsame Stellungnahmen und 19 Pressemitteilungen, die die Medien bald zu zitieren begannen. Am 4. April 2025 bestätigte das Verfassungsgericht schließlich einstimmig die Amtsenthebung des Präsidenten. Nach dem Amtsantritt der neuen Regierung im Juni 2025 schloss der Rat seine Arbeit mit einem Bericht ab, der seine Arbeit dokumentierte. Im Vorwort schreibt der Co-Vorsitzende Professor Kim Seon-Taek, dass die vergangenen acht Monate „eine Zeit waren, in der das Verfassungsrecht und auch die Verfassungsrechtswissenschaft ihre raison d’être unter Beweis stellen mussten“.
Jeong-In Yun ist Professorin an der Korea University und hat als Mitglied der Arbeitsgruppe des Rates den Bericht vorbereitet. Ich habe mit ihr über diesen „K-Scholactivism“ gesprochen.
1. War die Amtsenthebung von Präsident Yoon ein rechtlich eindeutiger Fall, oder ließ sich mit guten Gründen über das Urteil des Verfassungsgerichts streiten? Gibt es renommierte Wissenschaftler, die dem Urteil widersprachen?
Nach der südkoreanischen Verfassung setzt eine Amtsenthebung voraus, dass hochrangige Amtsträger:innen – einschließlich des Präsidenten – bei der Ausübung ihrer amtlichen Pflichten gegen die Verfassung oder das Gesetz verstoßen. Nach der ständigen Rechtsprechung des Verfassungsgerichts muss der Rechtsverstoß zudem ein hinreichendes Gewicht aufweisen. Es handelt sich um eine Art Verhältnismäßigkeitsprüfung.
Mit der Verhängung des Kriegsrechts hat Präsident Yoon seine Notstandsbefugnisse eindeutig verfassungswidrig überschritten. Er hat sich vollständig von den verfassungsrechtlichen Verfahren und materiellen Anforderungen hinweggesetzt. Unabhängig davon, ob darin zugleich eine strafbare Aufstandshandlung lag, war die Verfassungswidrigkeit der Kriegsrechtsverhängung eindeutig.
Darüber hinaus überschritten die Maßnahmen die Grenzen des geltenden Kriegsrechts. Sie untersagten sogar die Tätigkeit der Nationalversammlung, der kommunalen Organe und der politischen Parteien sowie jegliche politische Betätigung der Bürger:innen. Yoons Rechtsverstoß war also so offensichtlich und verfassungswidrig, dass das Amtsenthebungsverfahren nur folgerichtig war.
Was die nächste Frage betrifft: Ja, es gab auch Wissenschaftler, die sich gegen das Amtsenthebungsverfahren aussprachen. Sie sahen in der Verhängung des Kriegsrechts einen „acte de gouvernement“ („Regierungsakt“), ähnlich der Political-Question-Doktrin, der der Justiz entzogen sei. Andere erhoben verschiedene materielle und prozedurale Einwände, wie etwa die mangelnde Schwere der Amtsenthebungsgründe, unzureichende Beweise oder unzulässige Verfahrensabläufe. Das war jedoch nur eine kleine Minderheit der Wissenschaftler. Die lautstärksten unter ihnen gaben sehr aktiv Medieninterviews und reichten zudem Amicus-Curiae-Schriftsätze beim Verfassungsgericht ein. Der renommierteste unter ihnen war der emeritierte Professor Huh Young, ein prominenter Verfassungsrechtler, der in Deutschland Jura studiert hatte und seit den 1980er Jahren deutsche Verfassungstheorien in Südkorea einführte. Es war wirklich peinlich mitanzusehen, welche abwegigen Argumente ein angesehener, erfahrener Wissenschaftler zu diesen entscheidenden Fragen vortrug.
